title: Timing of Meals May Affect Brain Health
paragraphs: We often think about what we eat, but a new study from the United States suggests that when we eat may also be important, especially for the brain.
The study was led by Sue Shapses, a professor at Rutgers University. It was presented in July 2026 at NUTRITION 2026, a meeting of the American Society for Nutrition.

The study involved 47 women aged 50 to 79 who were overweight. All of them took part in a six-month weight-loss program and were asked to eat about 500 fewer calories a day. In addition, 26 of the women were asked to eat all of their food within a period of less than nine hours each day, usually between 10 a.m. and 6 p.m. This is known as "time-restricted eating." The other 21 women ate during their normal period of about 12 hours a day.

Both groups lost a similar amount of weight, about 15 pounds on average. However, the women who ate within the shorter time period did significantly better on tests of planning and problem-solving. They also made fewer mistakes on memory tests, although this difference was not large enough to be certain. In addition, the shorter the women's eating period, the more their thinking skills improved.

Because both groups lost the same amount of weight, the researchers believe that the timing of meals itself may have helped the brain. Shapses explained that losing weight alone can help protect against some decline in thinking skills with age, but eating within a shorter period may add an extra benefit. Shapses also suggested that people stop eating about four hours before going to bed.

However, the study was small, and it only included women who were overweight. Also, the results have not yet been fully reviewed by other scientists. The researchers say larger studies are needed before time-restricted eating can be recommended to improve brain health.
